Second, to clarify the practice of a bodhisattva means to practice the six perfections throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
From the past Śākyamuni Buddha to Kanakamuni Buddha, this period is called one asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
From this point on, he was forever free from a woman’s body; at that time, he did not know for himself whether he would become a Buddha or not.
Now it is said:

these are the five methods of settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*), the four applications of mindfulness through their distinct characteristics (*pṛthak-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*), and their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*).

By employing this contemplation of the mind to cultivate the *pāramitās*, at that time, although he has not yet produced the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) or understanding, he possesses compassion and vows, remains at peace within birth and death, and his mind is free from cowardice; thus, he is able to destroy the karma of a woman and constantly receives a male body.

At that time, as he had not yet generated the "warmth" of understanding (*ūṣmagata*), he remained at the stage of an external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*); therefore, he did not know for himself that his own body would become a Buddha.
Next, it is explained that from the time of Kāśyapa Śikhin Buddha until Dīpaṃkara Buddha constitutes two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

At that time, the Bodhisattva offered seven stalks of lotus flowers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha; he spread out his deerskin garment and laid his hair over the mud. Then, Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon him this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni."
At that time, although the Bodhisattva knew within himself, "I shall certainly become a Buddha," he did not verbally declare, "I shall become a Buddha.
This refers to attaining the wisdom of the *uṣmagata* stage and practicing the six *pāramitās*.
Next, it is explained that from the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha until Vipaśyin Buddha, the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa was completed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s inner mind was clearly realized, and he knew for himself that he would become a Buddha; he spoke these words of his own accord, free from any fear or hesitation:
"In a future age, I shall attain Buddhahood."
Now it is said:
this is the wisdom of the *mūrdhan* (Summit) stage, wherein one practices the six *pāramitās*.

Third, regarding the clarification that after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* one plants the karma for the thirty-two marks: now it is said this refers to entering the stage of *mṛdu-ksānti* (Lower Patience).
Employing this patience and wisdom, one practices the six perfections and accomplishes a hundred merits; using these hundred merits, one achieves a single mark.
In this manner, over the course of a hundred kalpas, one establishes the karmic causes for the thirty-two marks.
Fourth, the explanation of the fulfillment of the six *pāramitās*:

A bodhisattva is able to give everything, even not sparing his own body or life; as when King Śibi gave his body for the sake of the pigeon without feeling regret or resentment in his heart—this is the fulfillment of *dāna*.

The fulfillment of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) means maintaining the precepts without regard for one's own body or life, as King Sumati did. Through diligent observance of the precepts and constant reliance on truthful speech, he went to face death at the hands of King Mṛgāra; this is the fulfillment of śīla.

Regarding the fulfillment of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*): when a bodhisattva practices forbearance, not begrudging even their own body or life, as did the bhikṣu Kṣānti when King Kali cut him limb from limb; if he gives rise to a mind of compassionate endurance and makes a vow that his body shall be restored, this is called the fulfillment of patience.

The perfection of *vīrya-pāramitā* (diligence) is fulfilled when one exerts effort without sparing even body or life, as did the Crown Prince Mahādāna. For the sake of his subjects, he entered the sea to gather treasures and obtained a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
When a sea deity, while he was sleeping, stole the jewel and returned it to the ocean, the prince made a vow to bale out the seawater to recover the jewel for the sake of sentient beings.
Though he suffered until his life hung by a thread, his mind never faltered or retreated; this is called the fulfillment of diligence.

Regarding the fulfillment of the Dhyāna-pāramitā: it means that a bodhisattva is fully endowed with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and possesses mastery over entering and emerging from the meditative concentrations of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). For example, when the seer Śaṅkara was practicing seated meditation, he was without inhalation or exhalation; a bird nested in his topknot and hatched its young there, yet he remained unmoving out of compassion until the fledglings flew away. This is called the fulfillment of dhyāna.

Regarding the fulfillment of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is the discernment of the bodhisattva’s great mind; it is like the brahmin minister Govinda, who divided the great land of Jambudvīpa into seven parts, and likewise divided the various large cities, small cities, and villages into seven parts—the *prajñāpāramitā* is also like this.
This constitutes the fulfillment of the Bodhisattva’s six pāramitās.
It is now said that by means of this wisdom of "lower patience," one is able to subdue the sense faculties and bring the six perfections to completion.

Fifth, regarding those who dwell in the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood": this refers to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, who was born into the presence of Kāśyapa Buddha as a disciple in his final birth. There, he purely maintained the prohibitive precepts and practiced all manner of meritorious deeds; consequently, Kāśyapa Buddha bestowed upon him the prediction that he would next become a Buddha.
Now, it is said that this is still the stage of "intermediate patience" (*madhyā-kṣānti*).

Sixth, regarding the manifestation of birth in Tuṣita Heaven: having relinquished his retribution-body in Jambudvīpa, he is born above in this heaven to serve as the teacher of the devas; while remaining in that heaven, he cultivates the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhv-āyatanāni*).
Now it is said that this is still the stage of "intermediate patience" (madhyamā kṣānti). Question:
For what reason does a bodhisattva, upon first generating the mind of enlightenment, subdue the fetters (saṃyojana) without yet severing them?
Answer: If one were to sever the fetters, one would be unable to undergo birth and transformation as a manifested being (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The Bodhisattva contemplates impermanence to subdue the fetters, causing the fat of the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be consumed; by practicing the six perfections with a pure mind, he causes his various merits to flourish.

Seventh, regarding the clarification of attaining enlightenment through birth in the lower realm: this refers to the path of attaining bodhi through the eight phases as elucidated in the Tripiṭaka Teaching.
As for what are called the eight phases of attaining the Way: first, descending from Tuṣita Heaven;
second, entering the womb.
Third, birth; fourth, renunciation of the household life;
fifth, the subduing of Māra;
Sixth, the attainment of enlightenment;
seventh, the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
eighth, the entry into nirvana.
Question: Regarding the Tripiṭaka teachings elucidated here, the Abhidharma has its own gateways;
as for the exposition on the meaning of the Bodhisattva, is this the word of the Buddha?
Is this being taught by the śrāvaka disciples after the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa?
The answer is:
some of it was indeed spoken by the Buddha, while much of it consists of the explanations made by the various arhats in the *Vibhāṣā*.
Question: If this were spoken by the Buddha, it could be trusted;
but if it was spoken by the various arhats, how can it be trusted?
The answer is:
Since all Arhats are noble ones who have grasped the intent of the Buddha’s Tripiṭaka teachings to clarify the meaning of the Bodhisattva path, how could they possibly be so suddenly deviant?
Question:
If that is so, for what purpose does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refute [the opponent's views] point by point from beginning to end? Answer:
Nāgārjuna, wishing to expound the Mahāyāna and clarify the meaning of the Bodhisattva, refuted the Hīnayāna extensively; indeed, all [Hīnayāna views] may be refuted.
A questioner asks:
Nāgārjuna rebuked them, saying, "These disciples of Kātyāyanīputra have errors regarding the Hīnayāna sūtras," let alone their interpretation of the meaning of the Bodhisattva.
The answer is:

Śāriputra, even when the Buddha was in the world, there were still errors in the analytical discernment of the characteristics of dharmas; how much more so after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the case of the various arhats?
Although it is merely a shadowy semblance, it is still superior to the ordinary beings of the present age.

Third, regarding the explanation of the meanings of "pure," "stainless," and "renowned" according to the stages of the Tripiṭaka Teaching, this refers precisely to the stage of the "Middle Patience" (madhyakṣānti) as a candidate for Buddhahood (abhiṣekabhūmi).
The path of the six perfections is precisely the meaning of purity. Why is this so?
Within the three kinds of medicine, there are no three kinds of illness.
The six perfections are the Truth of the Path; this is the meaning of purity.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, seeing sons of the Buddha practicing various deeds and seeking unsurpassed wisdom, [the Buddha] preaches the pure path for them."
The Great Being Vimalakīrti has perfected the practice of the six *pāramitās*, which is the meaning of "pure" (*śuddha*);
because he is free from the defilements of the six obscurations, he is said to be "stainless" (*vimala*);

and by means of his conformative understanding, he internally accords with the principle of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing, while externally he accords with the conditions of the faculties, thereby assisting Śākyamuni Tathāgata in manifesting the teachings of the Three Vehicles; thus he is called "Pure," "Stainless," and "Accordant."

Therefore, in the "Expedient Means" chapter, he manifested illness and preached the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity to kings and elders; his intention was to reprove those people and exhort them to seek the fruit of Buddhahood.
Question:
Vimalakīrti refutes and subdues the śrāvakas and rebukes the bodhisattvas; this is the practice of the inconceivable stage.
How can one use the descriptions of the bodhisattva stages found in the Śrāvaka sūtras to compare and evaluate them?
The answer is:

A bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation is able to manifest in various ways; how could they not manifest the form of a bodhisattva as elucidated in the sūtras of the śrāvakas, to assist Śākyamuni in spreading the transformation of beings?
Question:
For what reason does he transform kings and elders and teach the Dharma by manifesting the form of a *tri-piṭaka* bodhisattva?
And why, when rebuking śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, does he immediately manifest the inconceivable teachings and words of the Mahāyāna?
The answer is:
Within the mundane realm, because fetters and karma have not yet been eliminated, the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing are taught; this is precisely the remedy for them.

For Arhats and Bodhisattvas, the afflictions within the mundane realm have already been removed, yet they remain deluded regarding the principle of the three inconceivable truths. Therefore, the three types of Four Noble Truths are taught to refute the Śrāvakas, while the Four Noble Truths of Non-action are taught to admonish the Bodhisattvas.

Second, regarding the explanation of the stages (*bhūmi*) according to the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya*), which clarifies "purity," "stainlessness," and "conformity to the stage": since this teaching elucidates the principle that dependent origination is itself emptiness, and all three vehicles equally receive its transmission, there must be degrees of depth in their realization of the principle and attainment of truth; therefore, it is necessary to distinguish these stages.

The entry into the Way through the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) likewise possesses four gates; here, we shall distinguish the stages according to the gate of emptiness (śūnyatā), which is further divided into three points:
first, a brief clarification of how the Three Vehicles are opened up according to the Shared Teaching;
second, a brief clarification of the stages of the Bodhisattva in the Shared Teaching.
Third, the explanation of the meanings of "pure," "stainless," and "renowned.

First, a brief clarification regarding those who open up the three vehicles according to the Shared Teaching: persons of the three vehicles equally receive the Shared Teaching and perceive the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the principle of non-conceptual true reality.
As for the analytical teaching of the three vehicles:

the Śrāvaka produces understanding from hearing; by grasping the general characteristics as being provisional, they enter into emptiness. Because their power of wisdom is weak, they sever only the active afflictions (*kleśa*).

The pratyekabuddha possesses merit and sharp faculties; being born in a world where no Buddha exists, they realize the provisional nature of reality spontaneously, yet their manifestation of the truth differs [from that of the bodhisattva].

Furthermore, it is explained that the pratyekabuddha, possessing sharp faculties, is able to discern the provisional nature of even slight distinct characteristics and enter emptiness; by manifesting true untainted wisdom, they sever the fetters of the three realms and attenuate and eliminate habitual tendencies.

Third, regarding those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle: Bodhisattvas cultivate wisdom of both general and specific characteristics, realizing that the essence of causes and conditions is emptiness; they give rise to great compassion and vows, and practice various Dharma gates.

If they perceive the ultimate truth (paramārtha), they sever the afflictions within the realms; yet, sustained by their vows, they return to birth within the three realms to exercise supernatural powers, mature sentient beings, and purify Buddha-lands.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"The Buddhas teach and transform sentient beings with the flavor of ambrosia; the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is this very flavor of ambrosia."
If one attains the true reality of all phenomena and extinguishes all afflictions, it is called the Śrāvaka-yāna;
if one gives rise to great compassion and conceives the unsurpassed resolve, it is called the Mahāyāna;
and if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha exists in the world, one generates wisdom through seclusion, it is called the Pratyekabuddha-yāna.
Second, regarding the clarification of the stages of the three vehicles according to the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya*), there are two points:
first, clarifying the ten stages common to the three vehicles;
second, distinguishing the names and specific positions within that shared framework.
First, regarding the clarification of the ten stages traversed in common by the three vehicles, there are two points:
first, the designation of their names;
second, a brief explanation.
First, the enumeration of names: first, the stage of dry wisdom;
second, the stage of nature;
third, the stage of the eight persons.
Fourth, the stage of seeing;
fifth, the stage of attenuation;
sixth, the stage of freedom from desire;
Seventh, the stage of those who have already accomplished their task;
eighth, the stage of the pratyekabuddhas;
ninth, the stage of the bodhisattvas.
Tenth is the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "From the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to the Bodhisattva grounds, the bodhisattva practices and studies them all, yet does not realize [the ultimate fruit]. On the Buddha-ground, one both studies and realizes; therefore, it is said that these constitute the common stages for the three vehicles.
Second, the brief explanation:
The stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) refers to the initial mind of the three vehicles; it is collectively termed the stage of dry wisdom.
This constitutes the level of the three worthies (*tri-piṭaka-arya*).
First, the five methods for settling the mind;
second, the mindfulness of specific characteristics;
third, the mindfulness of general characteristics.
These three stages are collectively termed the stage of external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana) and the ground of dry wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi). Question:
If this is so, what is the difference between these and the three grades of worthies (trayaḥ-satpuruṣa) as explained in the Tripiṭaka teaching?

Answer: Superficially, the names are the same; however, regarding the two modes—the clumsy and the skillful—they have already been distinguished in the previous analysis of the three contemplations. How could they not be different?
Question:

Since practitioners of the Three Vehicles equally contemplate the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), they should likewise equally destroy the eight inversions and equally perceive the Buddha-nature; how then can it be said that those of the Shared Teaching enter into the two types of nirvana?
Answer: To say that "shattering the eight inversions" is a provisional statement; when analyzed, there are four different types:

first, shattering the eight inversions without binding them to the concepts of withering or flourishing—this means it cannot yet be definitively categorized as *tong* (Shared), *bie* (Distinct), or *yuan* (Perfect).
Second, by destroying the eight inversions and concluding with the four "withered" aspects, it primarily belongs to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
Third, by destroying the eight inversions and concluding with the four "flourishing" aspects, it definitively constitutes the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
Fourth, the subversion of the eight inversions, which simultaneously concludes the themes of withering and flourishing, constitutes the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Herein we clarify the subversion of the eight inversions by employing Vimalakīrti’s reprimand of Kātyāyana: he refutes the five meanings of the Tripitaka and expounds the five meanings of the Mahāyāna, thereby concluding the formation of the four aspects of withering.
Therefore, those bhikṣus whose minds have attained liberation belong, for the most part, to the meaning of the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-śāsana).

Second, to clarify the Stage of Nature (gotrabhūmi): if, by means of the general characteristics of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), one first gives rise to wholesome, out-flowing (sāsrava) five aggregates, this is called the Dharma of Heat (uṣmagata).

Advancing through the initial, middle, and final stages of mind, one enters the stages of the Peak (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (laukikāgradharma); these are all termed the "inner ordinary beings of the nature-ground" (xingdi neifan), as they collectively suppress the afflictions of views within the realms.

Third, regarding the clarification of the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*): this refers to practitioners of both the two types—those who follow by faith and those who follow the Dharma—within the Three Vehicles. Through skillful contemplation, they give rise to the truth while abiding in the state of the "uninterrupted samādhi" (*ānantarya-samādhi*), the fifteen moments of mind, and the eight patiences (*kṣānti*).

Fourth, regarding the clarification of the stage of insight (*darśana-bhūmi*): this refers to the three vehicles collectively perceiving the principle of the first meaning—the Four Noble Truths of non-arising—and collectively severing the delusions of view, namely the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).

Fifth, the Stage of Thinness (Tanubhūmi): the substance of craving is understood as being identical to the ultimate truth; one gives rise to six grades of unimpeded wisdom, abandons the six grades [of afflictions] of the desire realm, realizes the sixth liberation, and thus the afflictions of the desire realm become thin.

Sixth, the stage of detachment from desire refers to those of the three vehicles who realize that the substance of craving is itself the provisional and thus the true; they exhaustively sever the five lower fetters of the desire realm and thereby become detached from the afflictions of the desire realm.

Seventh, the Stage of Having Accomplished (Kṛtāvī-bhūmi): this refers to those of the Three Vehicles who realize that the essence of form and the realm of formlessness is itself true; they give rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), sever the five higher fetters (*pañcordhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), and exhaust the seventy-two grades [of afflictions].
Because one has brought about the ultimate severance of the delusions of the three realms, it is called the "Stage of Having Accomplished What Was to Be Done" (Kṛtāvī-bhūmi).

Eighth, regarding the stage of the Pratyekabuddha: because the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas have given rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), their power of merit is great, and they are thus able to erode and eliminate residual habits (*vāsanā*).

9. Regarding the Bodhisattva Stage (*bodhisattvabhūmi*): Having entered from emptiness into the contemplation of the provisional, one’s practice becomes fully matured. With the dual flow of the path and contemplation, one deeply contemplates the two truths. Advancing to sever residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) as well as the non-cognition regarding form and mind, one attains the Dharma-eye and the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*). One sports with supernormal powers, purifies Buddha-fields, and studies all Buddha-dharmas such as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and great compassion; at this stage, the habit-energies are about to be exhausted.

Tenth, regarding the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*): through the power of great merit and its support of wisdom, one attains the wisdom of instantaneous correspondence (*ekakṣaṇa-samāyukta-prajñā*), which illuminates both the ultimate and the conventional truths to their furthest extent, such that all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) within all realms are completely exhausted.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The power of wisdom of the śrāvakas is weak, like a small fire burning wood; although the wood is consumed, charcoal still remains.
The power of wisdom of the pratyekabuddhas is superior, like a great fire burning wood; the wood is incinerated and the charcoal exhausted, yet ashes remain."

"The wisdom-power of all Buddhas is great, like the fire at the end of a kalpa that consumes both charcoal and ash," which is also like the parable of the three animals—the hare, the horse, and the elephant—crossing a river.
Question: The names "Bodhisattva" and "Buddha-stage" differ from those of the Two Vehicles; how can you say they are common to them? Answer:

Although their names differ, they are equally those beyond training (aśaikṣa) and worthy of offerings (arhat); having attained the two types of nirvāṇa, they both return to the extinction of the ashes; as the realization of the fruit is one, there is no difference in their meaning or designation.
Thus, both the name and its meaning are ultimately identical.
Second, regarding the clarification that while the names differ, the stages are common, there are two points:
first, concerning the ten stages common to the three vehicles prior, the Bodhisattva establishes the specific name "Patience" (kṣānti).
Second, using the terminology of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), the names are distinct while the meanings are universal.

First, regarding the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) practiced in common by the three vehicles, the specific names of "patience" (*kṣānti*) are established for Bodhisattvas. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Bodhisattva dharma, the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) is called 'Patience of Subduing' (*vinaya-kṣānti*);
the Stage of Nature (*gotrabhūmi*) is called 'Patience of Accordance' (*anuloma-kṣānti*)."
The stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*) is, in the Dharma of the bodhisattva, called the name of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-nāman*);
the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) is, in the Dharma of the bodhisattva, called the fruit of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti-phala*);
the stage of refinement (*tanu-bhūmi*) is, in the Dharma of the bodhisattva, called the purity of freedom from desire (*vairāgya-viśuddhi*).
The stage of detachment from desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*) is called the "play of supernormal powers" (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*) within the Bodhisattva-dharma;

the stage of having completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*) is designated as the "Buddha-stage" (*buddha-bhūmi*) in the Śrāvaka sūtras. The stages of the Pratyekabuddha and up to the Buddha-stage are to be distinguished as previously explained.
Question:
For what reason are distinct names such as "subduing patience" (伏忍) established separately within the dharma of the bodhisattvas? Answer:
Although the contemplation of principle is the same, there are differences in the skillful means of practice for transforming others and in the pursuit of the fruit of Buddhahood;
therefore, distinct names such as "subduing patience" (*kṣānti*) and so forth are established separately within the Bodhisattva dharma.
The detailed analysis of these characteristics is fully contained in the fourfold teaching of the *Mohe zhiguan*.

Second, regarding the use of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) terminology where the names are distinct but the meanings are universal: this refers to the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) which the three vehicles observe in common; it is the Bodhisattva’s use of the ten stages of faith, the thirty minds, and the ten grounds of the Distinct Teaching to distinguish their respective positions.
The Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi) corresponds to the Patience of Subduing (vinīyaka-kṣānti), which is established as the specific name for the Ten Faiths (daśa-śraddhā).

The Stage of Nature (gotra-bhūmi) corresponds to the Patience of Accordance (anuloma-kṣānti), which is established as the names for the Ten Abidings (daśa-vihāra), the Ten Practices (daśa-caryā), and the Ten Transferences (daśa-pariṇāmanā).

The stage of the eight persons and the stage of vision are precisely the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); thus, the stage of joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) is established. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"The wisdom and abandonment of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) is the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas."
The stage of the Srotāpanna is the stage of "Leaving Defilement" (Vimalā-bhūmi), and its fruit is the stage of "Luminosity" (Prabhākārī-bhūmi). Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"The knowledge and abandonment of a Sakṛdāgāmin constitute the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
The stage and fruit of the Anāgāmin: the stage is the Arciṣmatī-bhūmi, and the fruit is the Sudurjayā-bhūmi. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"The knowledge and abandonment of the Anāgāmin constitute the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."

The stage of the Arhat’s path and its fruit correspond to the Present Stage (*Pratyutpanna-bhūmi*), while its fruition corresponds to the Far-Reaching Stage (*Dūraṅgama-bhūmi*). Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"The wisdom and abandonment of an Arhat constitute the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
The stage of the Pratyekabuddha is precisely the eighth Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi), wherein the residual habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are eradicated; thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"The wisdom and abandonment of a Pratyekabuddha constitute the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
The Bodhisattva-bhūmi consists of the nine Śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmis;
the tenth, the Dharmameghā-bhūmi, should be understood as being like the Buddha-bhūmi.

The Buddha-bhūmi is as previously described. At the time of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the wisdom of single-moment correspondence (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*) exhausts all residual impressions (*vāsanā*), namely the residual impressions of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstructions to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Having completed the transformation of all sentient beings with whom they have a karmic connection, they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder), like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted; the eight phases of attaining the Way are as previously explained.

Thus, although the names used to distinguish the stages differ from those of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-vidyā*), their meaning is the same; these still belong to the explanation of the Bodhisattva stages according to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-vidyā*).
Question:
From the first stage (bhūmi) to the seventh stage, in what sutras or treatises are these contrasted with the four fruits of the śramaṇa?
Answer: [As follows:]
The various sutras and treatises are not without their points of correspondence, though they differ in their levels of profundity;
likewise, the correspondences established by Dharma masters of past and present are often diverse.
The reason for this is that some claim that the stage of insight (*darśana-bhūmi*) corresponds only to the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), which is the position currently adopted.

Some take the third stage as being combined with and corresponding to the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*); the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* clarifies that the fourth stage is combined with and corresponds to the stage of seeing. This, however, is difficult to rely upon as a definitive standard.

Yet, in the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śikṣā*), the stage of seeing is fundamentally the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*); one does not emerge from contemplation to realize the fruit of *srotāpanna*. How, then, could one abandon the delusions of seeing starting from the first stage, and continue through the third—or even the fourth—stage!
If the Separate Teaching (biejiao) clarifies that the severance of distinct delusions is not equal to that of the Two Vehicles, such an explanation may indeed exist.

Furthermore, some say, "The severance of fetters at the sixth stage is equal to that of an Arhat," while others say, "The seventh stage is named Arhat"; these claims are difficult to take as fixed dogmas.
Since the meanings of the two fruits— preceding and succeeding— are not definitively established in the sūtras and śāstras,
the two intermediate fruits may be understood through inference.
As they cannot be fixedly relied upon, I shall now employ logical reasoning to establish this correspondence of stages.
Although one may briefly pass through it, one must ultimately not grasp it.

Third, regarding the explanation of the stages according to the Shared Teaching (Prajñāpāramitā), as for the meanings of "Pure," "Undefiled," and "Worthy": the stage of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) at the position of the Future Buddha (Upapatti-bhūmi) has a principle of ultimate truth that is inherently luminous; thus it is called "Pure.
Because the two obstacles and their primary delusions within the realm of desire have been exhausted, while residual habit-energies are but slight, it is called "Undefiled."

Internally, their wisdom accords with ultimate truth; externally, they can adapt to the capacities of the three vehicles through supernatural powers and preaching the Dharma; hence, they are said to be "conforming.
This briefly explains how the Mahāsattvas of the Shared Teaching receive the names "Pure," "Undefiled," and "Conforming."

The reason for manifesting this form of a bodhisattva is to use this appearance and voice to feign illness, thereby preaching the Dharma that all things are like dreams and illusions to kings and elders, and exhorting them to seek Bodhi.
Furthermore, they refute the Three-Vehicle teachings of the Tripiṭaka, clinging to the delusions and deviations of crude expedients.
If one examines the commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* by Master Kumārajīva, Daosheng, and Sengzhao, they all employ this same intention;

yet when the various great Dharma Masters of the Liang and Chen dynasties lectured on the text of this sūtra and judged the stages of the Bodhisattvas, their interpretations regarding the relative heights and depths of these positions, though slightly different, [all accord with this].
Looking back at the various schools of our own tradition, they all interpret this sutra solely through the perspective of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao).

Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning of "Stainless" (*vimalā*) and "Renowned" (*yaśas*) by way of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao): this teaching universally elucidates the principle of the provisional name, such as the Tathāgatagarbha and Buddha-nature. Since Bodhisattvas receive this teaching and practice until they attain realization, proceeding from the shallow to the deep, it is necessary to clarify the stages (*bhūmi*).

This distinct teaching (biejiao) for entering the Way also possesses four gates; here, we shall clarify the stages of practice and position (xingwei) solely by way of the gates of emptiness and existence.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"The emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā) is called Buddha-nature."
"The wise perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness;
the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas perceive only emptiness and do not perceive non-emptiness.
That which is "non-empty" is precisely the Buddha-nature.

Third, explaining "purity," "stainlessness," and "conformity to the meaning" according to the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).

First, regarding the differentiation of the bodhisattva stages in the sutras and treatises according to the Distinct Teaching: one should investigate how the Distinct Teaching correctly elucidates the principle of the provisional names of causes and conditions, the *sands-of-the-Ganges* of Buddha-dharmas, and True Suchness-Buddha-nature. Bodhisattvas who receive this teaching contemplate the principle of the three truths and practice through successive kalpas, severing the *sands-of-the-Ganges* of ignorance and the distinct afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), desiring to see Buddha-nature and seeking the eternal nirvana of the four virtues.
Now, to clarify that the distinct stages differ, they are briefly categorized into three points:
first, the number of stages elucidated in various sutras differs;
second, the hierarchy of their abandonment and subdual of afflictions differs.
Third, differences regarding the gates of the Dharma (*abhidharma*).

First, as for the differences in the number of stages (*bhūmi*) clarified in various sutras: for instance, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* lists the thirty minds, the ten stages, and the Buddha stage, totaling forty-one positions;
the *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* (Yingluo jing) clarifies that there are fifty-two positions.
The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) elucidates fifty-one stages;

the newly translated *Jinguangming jing* (Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra), the *Shengtianwang banruo jing* (Tathāgatagarbha-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra), and the *Dapin jing* (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) only elucidate the ten bhūmis and the Buddha-bhūmi, without opening up the thirty minds.
The *Daban niepan jing* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra) elucidates the five practices and the meaning of the ten merits, which, when extended, open up the thirty minds and the ten bhūmis.
The various treatises clarify the stages and positions (bhūmi), which differ in their number; this is because they are all based on different sūtras.
Second, regarding the differences in the levels of abandonment and suppression: the twenty moments of mind abandon the fetters within the realm of desire, differing in their respective heights;

the ten stages abandon the views and afflictions outside the realm, with variations according to their corresponding positions. These details are fully contained in the fundamental texts of the Four Teachings.
Third, regarding the differences in the presentation of the dharma-gates: for example, in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the ten pāramitās are correlated with the ten practices;
whereas in the newly translated *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, the ten pāramitās are correlated with the ten stages (bhūmis).
In this manner, these various sutras differ greatly in how they correlate stages with the various dharma-gates.
Question:
For what reason do the distinct teachings clarify the stages, while the sutras and treatises differ in their enumeration and correlation with the dharma-gates?
Answer:

The Separate Teaching (biejiao) distinguishes the ten stages, practices, abandonments, and suppressions outside the realms, employing various dharma-gates, *siddhāntas*, and skillful means to guide and attract beings according to their capacities; therefore, it is largely indeterminate.
Second, a brief explanation of the stages of the Bodhisattva according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao): now, based on the *Ābhūṣaṇa-sūtra*, it is explained that there are seven kinds of stages:
first, the ten faiths (shixin);
second, the ten abidings (shizhu).
Third, the ten practices;
fourth, the ten dedications;
fifth, the ten stages.
Sixth, the Stage of Equal Enlightenment;
seventh, the Stage of Sublime Enlightenment.
First, regarding the stage of the Ten Faiths: the names and meanings of these ten faiths are fully contained in the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra].

Now, it is explained that the Bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching believes in the Buddha-nature of causes and conditions and the eternal Three Jewels; knowing the immeasurable and unconditioned Four Noble Truths, they give rise to compassion and the four great vows. Being unable to be obstructed by celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, or those of the Two Vehicles, this is called "faith."

If one looks to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the clarification of the five practices, these consist of the holy practice of precepts (*śīla-āryacaryā*) and the holy practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi-āryacaryā*).

Cultivating the holy practice of wisdom (*prajñā-āryacaryā*) regarding the four truths of arising and ceasing to subdue the delusions of views within the realm of desire constitutes the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-citta*).
Question:

Since Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) have already taken as their object the immeasurable and unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) Four Noble Truths when they resolve upon *bodhicitta*, for what reason do they cultivate the contemplation of the four noble truths of arising and ceasing (*utpādanirodha*)?
Answer:

Although a bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) initially believes in the principle of the immeasurable and unconditioned Four Noble Truths, their afflictive hindrances within the realm of desire are heavy; they must therefore first sever these delusions. For this reason, they first cultivate the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing to harmonize the mind.

Second, regarding the clarification of the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*): these correspond to the nature of the seeds of practice (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*), which is the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*).
The wisdom that enters into principle is termed "abiding.

As for what is meant by "entering into principle," it refers to entering directly into the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*), which resembles the entry into the true principle of the Perfect Truth (*pūrṇa-satya*).
If one looks toward the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, this is precisely the cultivation of the contemplation of the four noble truths of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Here, however, we clarify that these ten stages (*bhūmi*) all consist of cultivating the contemplation of entering emptiness through the provisional nature of the body, thereby giving rise to the wisdom of partial truth (*ekadeśatattva*), severing the views and afflictions within the realm of desire, attaining the eye of all-encompassing wisdom, and generating an understanding of the semblance Middle Way; this is precisely the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) in the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra-yāna*).
Third, regarding the clarification of the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), this refers to the nature-seed-nature (*prakṛti-gotra*).
Having previously clarified the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), wherein one has already attained entry into principle;

now, arising from that principle to initiate practice, one studies the ten *pāramitās*, and thus it is called the "ten practices. In relation to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, this corresponds to the meditative gate of practicing the contemplation of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths.

Now, it is explained that the cultivation of the Ten Practices involves entering the contemplation from emptiness into the provisional (shikṣā-prativedha). One severs the ignorance as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attains the wisdom of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā), and acquires the Dharma-eye. Within the realm of desire, the active afflictions (paryavasthāna) are already exhausted; the understanding of the semblance Middle Way gradually becomes clearer and more distinct—this is precisely the stage of the "Summit" (mūrdhan) in the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddhayāna).
Fourth, regarding the clarification of the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*): these constitute the nature of the path-seeds (*mārga-bīja*).

When the mind of understanding and practice merges, one dedicates causes toward the fruit and proceeds in accordance with the Dharma-realm; hence they are called "dedication. In relation to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, this should correspond to the cultivation of the contemplation of the four noble truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Here, however, it clarifies that this Bodhisattva cultivates the correct contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). As the understanding of the Middle Way becomes increasingly clear and bright, he is able to subdue ignorance and attain a semblance of the Buddha-eye of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*); this is precisely the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) within the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*).
Question:
Since you have already clarified the stages of the distinct teaching (biejiao), what is the purpose of correlating them with the levels of Heat (nǎn), Summits (dǐng), and Patience (rěn)? Answer:

Since the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) correspond to the four fruits and the thirty mental states (*triṃśac-citta*), how could they not also correspond to the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*)?
Question:
Since these are Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching, how can they cultivate the contemplative gate of the unconditioned Four Noble Truths (*anabhisaṃskṛta-catur-āryasatya*)?
Answer: This matter is complex and its implications are difficult to resolve.
It is fully contained within the original texts; how could one expect to reach a definitive conclusion immediately?
Fifth, regarding the clarification of the ten stages (*bhūmi*): these are the stages of the noble lineage (*āryagotra*).

From entering the first stage, one immediately awakens to the truth and clearly perceives the Buddha-nature and the equal *dharmadhātu*. Abiding in its own essence, it gives rise to the merits of all Buddhas and is capable of bearing the burden of all sentient beings; therefore, they are called "stages."

If one looks toward the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it should be that [the practitioner] has partially realized the principle of the four noble truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), attained the twenty-five samādhis called the "Kings of Samādhis," fulfilled the five practices, and successively accomplished the ten merits and entered the ten stages; I suspect this is what is intended here.
Now, to clarify this stage of the Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds:

upon ascending the first ground, one immediately realizes the ultimate truth of the true Middle Way and simultaneously illuminates the two truths. With every thought-moment, there is tranquil extinction, and one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). One is able to sever the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), partially attaining the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the Buddha-eye, and attaining the two bodies of the Tathāgata—the True Body and the Responsive Body—to perform transformative teachings throughout the ten directions.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage, ignorance (*avidyā*) is severed throughout; however, based on their respective positions, they are divided into three paths:
the first stage is called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*);
the second through the sixth stages are called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
From the seventh stage onward, it is called the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
The masters of the *Dilun* school say:
"The second through the seventh stages are called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)."
"From the eighth stage onward, it is called the Path of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣamārga).
That the Bodhisattva of the first stage is endowed with the five practices likely refers to the merits of the first stage.
As for the remaining nine kinds of merit, they may correspond to the [remaining] nine stages."

Regarding the statement that one destroys ignorance and the specific delusions of view, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "From this point onward, all are called people of wrong views. This means that those of the Three Vehicles within the Tripiṭaka and the Shared Teachings have not yet perceived this principle; therefore, they are called people of wrong views.
The Great Being rebuked Subhūti, intending to convey that the Great Teacher is your teacher, whereas the celestial Māras and non-Buddhist heretics act as your companions in toil.

Even up to the ten stages of faith and the thirty minds of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), although these delusions are suppressed, they have not yet been severed; thus, one still possesses the distinct views of ignorance (avidyā). It may be that the intention behind the censure of the bodhisattvas lies precisely here.

Second, from the second bhūmi to the sixth bhūmi, one is called a practitioner of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), who severs the specific delusions and the craving of the three realms. As clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, when Kāśyapa heard the sound of the ciṅkāra lute, he could not remain composed; Kāśyapa said, "I have already severed the five desires of the three realms."

"These are the five desires produced by the pure and sublime merits of a bodhisattva; therefore, one cannot find peace within these matters. This applies equally to craving for the realm of form and the formless realm.
In this sutra, the Great Being rebukes Subhūti, saying: "You are the same as those with afflictions; you have not reached the other shore.
You have entered the eight difficulties; you have not attained freedom from difficulty. This is the intended meaning.
Therefore, from the second stage through the sixth stage, they are collectively termed the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), wherein these specific delusions are abandoned.
Now, inferring by way of meaning:

the second stage, the Ground Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), involves the initial penetration and abandonment of the specific desire-attachment of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), and is thus named the candidate for the stage of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
The third stage, the Ground of the Three Knowledges (*trividyā*), corresponds to the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*).
The fourth stage, the Ground of the Four Blazes (*caturjvālā*), corresponds to the path toward the fruit of *anāgāmin* in the Separate Teaching.
The fifth stage, the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), corresponds to the fruit of *anāgāmin* in the Separate Teaching, wherein the separate craving and desire are completely severed.

The sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), corresponds to the candidate for Arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*) in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-śāsana*), wherein one severs the specific attachments to the realms of form and formlessness.

The seventh stage, the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*), corresponds to the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattva-phala*) in the Separate Teaching; because one has completely severed all specific attachments to the realms of form and formlessness, it is from this point onward termed the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
Question: In response to these four fruits, from which sutras or treatises are they derived? Answer: [They are derived from] the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.
In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), the clarification of the severance and suppression [of afflictions] in relation to the four fruits varies greatly across the sūtras and śāstras;
the methods employed by the various Mahāyāna masters are likewise diverse. Regarding the classification of stages according to the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), the Dilun masters state:

"The first stage severs views; the second stage severs desire for the realm of form (*kāmadhātu*); the third stage severs desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); and the fourth stage severs desire for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding the classification of stages according to the Fundamental School (*tongzong*) of the Dilun masters, there is a tradition that uses: "The third stage severs views and is named *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer)..."
"From the fourth stage to the sixth stage, one is called a Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner), the second teacher of reliance;
from the seventh stage to the ninth stage, one is called an Anāgāmin (Non-returner), the third teacher of reliance;

the tenth stage and Equal Enlightenment are called Arhats, the fourth teacher of reliance. Some say, "One severs [delusions of] views at the third stage, the fourth stage is named Sakṛdāgāmin, the fifth stage is named Anāgāmin, and the sixth stage is named Arhat. Others follow the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), which states, "One severs views at the fourth stage, the fifth stage is named Sakṛdāgāmin, the sixth stage is named Anāgāmin, and the seventh stage is named Arhat. Because such divergent explanations differ, it is difficult to rely upon any one of them definitively.
Now, inferring by way of principle, this [interpretation] is formulated as a response to the four fruits of the path.
At first glance it seems convenient, yet since there is no explicit textual authority, the Buddha’s intention is difficult to discern; one need not dogmatically cling to it.
Question: For what reason is the explanation considered indeterminate? Answer:
This has already been explained as before.
The eighth stage, the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), is the stage of the *pratyekabuddha* according to the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*).
The masters of the *Dilun* school state, "From this point onward, the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is elucidated," though it is unknown from which sūtra or śāstra this is derived.

Not only does one attain the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) in the eighth stage, but while remaining in quiescence, there is constant functioning; and while functioning, there is no appearance of marks. Through this effortless mind, the ignorance and delusions of the dharma-realm are naturally severed, and the habitual tendencies of form are exhausted.

The ninth stage, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*), is characterized by the slight attenuation of ignorance; the habitual tendencies of the mind are completely severed, wisdom becomes increasingly clear and distinct, and one skillfully enters into the true nature of reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
The tenth stage, the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*), possesses compassion and wisdom that are like a great cloud;
its compassion universally moistens all beings, raining down the rain of Dharma upon everything.
The Cloud of Wisdom is able to sustain the rain of Dharma preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions and cuts off the ten grades of ignorance.
Sixth, the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samudāgama-bhūmi) is the fulfillment of the wisdom of the ultimate limit, entering the gate of profound mystery.
If one looks toward the Cloud of Dharma, they are called a Buddha;
if one looks toward Wondrous Enlightenment, they are called a Bodhisattva of the Vajra Mind, also known as a Bodhisattva of the Stainless Ground.
The three maras have already been exhausted, with only the single category of the mara of death remaining, which is the severing of the habitual tendencies of ignorance.
Question:
Why was the Buddha of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambuddha) not distinguished in the preceding Shared Teaching (Pāryāya-yāna)? Answer:

Because the habitual tendencies within the realms (*dhātu*) are easily exhausted, there is no need to posit the stage of Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā*) or the emergence of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Question:

Why is it that in certain places within the sutras and treatises of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), after explaining the stage of Dharma-Cloud, there is further mention of the Vajra [Stage] and Equal Enlightenment?
There are existing sutras and treatises that clarify only that once the practices of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are perfected, one immediately attains the fruit of Buddhahood.
Regarding this, the Dharma masters of the North and South have engaged in much contentious debate.
In response, it is said:
Furthermore, the establishment of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) is not yet fixed as an obstacle.

The reason for this is that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies that the merit and wisdom of the tenth stage, Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), when compared to that of a Buddha, is like the soil on a fingernail compared to the great earth.
If that is so, although one speaks of a single category (*pakṣa*) of ignorance, in reality it cannot be said to consist of categories.
How is this known?

For the Bodhisattva in his final mind, on the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*), his speed is swifter than the wind; in a single day, he is able to shatter immeasurable categories of the obscurations and delusions of ignorance.

How much more so for the *Āṭānāṭīya-sūtra* (or *Ratnavyūha-sūtra*), which clarifies the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*). Having entered the gate of profound mystery over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one practices the affairs of ordinary beings in reverse.

Therefore, it opens the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) and further establishes the Buddha of Equal Enlightenment with the Vajra-mind; this is not erroneous from the perspective of principle.

If one knows that within a single grade there are immeasurable grades of ignorance, which are exhausted by the unimpeded wisdom of the Cloud of Dharma stage, then why would it be necessary to further establish the stage of Equal Enlightenment?

The stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*) refers to the mind following the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*); it is the luminous and great awakening where wondrous wisdom exhausts the source, the habitual tendencies of ignorance are extinguished, and this is called liberation.
Being serene and free from all burdens, tranquil yet ever-illuminating, it is called the stage of wondrous enlightenment.
Abiding eternally in the fruit of Buddhahood and being fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, it is called the fruit of bodhi.
The nirvana of the four virtues is called the "fruit of fruits. Question:
Is it definitively by means of vajra-wisdom that ignorance is severed?
Is it by means of wondrous enlightenment that one cuts off ignorance?
The answer is:
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "One who has something to cut off is called a superior person (sopadhiśeṣa)."
"One who has nothing further to be severed is called the Unsurpassed One.
[The interlocutor] asks:
For what reason does the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* state that "the ground of the dwelling of ignorance possesses the greatest power, and it is that which can be severed by the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom"?
Answer:
If one uses the distinct [path] to connect with the fruition, then the ten stages and the stage of Equal Enlightenment are themselves the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom. Why is this so?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas in the ninth stage are said to 'see by hearing';
Bodhisattvas in the tenth stage are said to 'see with the eye. Although they see the Buddha-nature, their vision is not yet clear."
Because the path of non-obstruction coexists with afflictions, it is not clear and distinct.
That which the Buddhas and Tathāgatas perceive with complete clarity is true liberation, utterly transcending all burdens; therefore, it is clear and distinct.

If one explains the meaning according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), from the initial stage of Joy (huanxi), one employs the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom to sever the first grade of ignorance, continuing until the final thought-moment of Equal Enlightenment (dengjue), at which point it is finally severed entirely.

According to the explicit teaching of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), this refers to the first stage of the Bodhisattva path, the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (Prathamacittotpādavihāra), where one attains the wisdom of the Buddha's Bodhi and severs the first grade of ignorance, continuing until the final thought-moment of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), at which point it is finally exhausted.

Third, regarding the explanation of "Pure," "Stainless," and "Renowned" according to the stages of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*): since Vimalakīrti is a Great Being (*mahāsattva*) in his final birth before Buddhahood, he is the Dharma-body itself, abiding in the stage of the Stainless Bodhisattva at the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) of Equal Enlightenment (*samayaksaṃbodhi*).
Because the principle of Buddha-nature is manifest, it is called "Pure" (śuddha).

Because both the fundamental and habitual afflictions of the specific delusions have been exhausted, and even the residual traces of ignorance are like thin smoke—existing yet as if non-existent—it is called "Stainless" (vimala).

Because the wisdom of the ultimate limit is perfected, internally corresponding to the profound principle while externally functioning without fixed direction, such that one accords with conditions to perform transformative teachings within the equality of the Dharma-realm, it is called "Conformity" (prabhāsvara). Thus, they are termed Pure, Stainless, and Conformity.
How could this be the same as the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings, which distinguish purity, stainlessness, and the meaning of the name!

The reason the traces of the teaching appear identical to the stage of the "One More Birth" (Ekajātipratibaddha) is to censure the three vehicles of the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings, and to gather in the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching Mahāyāna.
Mysterious Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Three;
Mysterious Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhiyi of Xiuchan Temple on Mount Tiantai.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the meanings of "Pure," "Stainless," and "Renowned" by way of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*):

this teaching elucidates the principle of the single ultimate truth (*ekasatyam*), inconceivable liberation, the Buddha-nature like space, Great Parinirvāṇa, and the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of all Buddhas, which is dependent origination itself.
If a bodhisattva receives this teaching, although its principle is neither deep nor shallow, there are nonetheless levels of depth and shallowness for those who realize it.
Now, to clarify how one enters the Way through this teaching, it likewise possesses four gates; however, most Mahāyāna sūtras predominantly employ the "gate of neither emptiness nor existence."

Just as in this sutra, each of the bodhisattvas speaks of "entering the gate of non-duality"; while they are generally the same at first glance, upon careful examination, there is no lack of distinction among four gates, though most employ the "neither-empty-nor-existent gate" to enter inconceivable liberation.
This meaning will naturally become clear further below; for now, it shall be briefly presented under three headings:
first, distinguishing the differences in the delineation of stages between the Separate and Perfect Teachings;
second, the formal elucidation of the delineation of stages within this teaching.
Third, regarding the stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), I shall explain the meanings of "pure," "non-existent," and "stainless.

First, to distinguish the differences in the elucidation of stages between the Perfect and the Two [Partial] Teachings: since the Perfect Teaching expounds the perfect principle, it briefly clarifies eight aspects of the perfect meaning that differ from the eight distinct [partial] teachings, as already explained previously;
here, however, we shall simply focus on the differences in the levels of attainment based on the severance of ignorance (*avidyā*).

According to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the thirty minds sever the fetters within the realm of desire; this simultaneously suppresses the ignorance beyond the realm. Upon reaching the final mind of the stage of Dedication (huixiang), one gives rise to true wisdom, perceives the principle of the Middle Way—the Buddha-nature—and severs the first grade of ignorance, which is called "ascending to the First Ground" (prathamā-bhūmi).
Continuing in this manner until the tenth grade of ignorance is severed is called the "Tenth Ground" (daśamī-bhūmi).
Only at the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-sambodhi) is ignorance completely exhausted.
The wondrous enlightenment is serene and detached from all burdens; this is as previously analyzed.

According to what is elucidated in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), from the very first moment of generating the mind through provisional names, one practices the three contemplations within a single mind, cultivates the mind of sympathetic joy, and enters the stage of the ten faiths (*shixin*). Therein, by severing all afflictions within the realm of desire (*jie-nei huo*), one simultaneously suppresses the ignorance (*wuming*) beyond that realm.
At the initial mind of the ten abidings (*shizhu*), one gives rise to the perfect true wisdom and severs the first grade of ignorance.
From these forty stages of mind, ignorance is severed at each level until it is finally exhausted at the final moment of the stage of Equal Enlightenment;
at the ultimate ground of Sublime Enlightenment, one is serenely detached from all burdens, which is termed the ultimate Bodhi and the Unsurpassed Great Nirvana.
This constitutes a judgment of stages, wherein there are distinct differences in rank; thus, the two teachings of Distinct and Perfect differ in their clarification of the stages.
Second, as for the formal clarification of the stages of the Perfect Teaching, this likewise proceeds by means of seven categories to clarify the differences among the fifty-two stages:
first, the ten faiths;
Second, the ten abodes;
third, the ten practices;
fourth, the ten dedications.
Fifth, the stage of the ten bhūmis;
sixth, the stage of equal enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi);
seventh, the stage of wondrous enlightenment (pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna).

However, interpretations differ; some masters state: "In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there is sudden awakening; once awakened, one is immediately a Buddha, with no further distinctions of stages.
The teaching of the ten stages is intended only for those of dull faculties."

As the *Siksāsamuccaya-sūtra* states: "One who studies in this manner does not proceed from one stage to another. Furthermore, there are masters who explain: "Since the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is characterized by sudden enlightenment (*dunwu*), a single awakening at the initial stage constitutes ultimate and perfect consummation."
As for the existence of forty-two stages, these are merely skillful means for transforming sentient beings, established as names for shallow and deep levels.
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The first stage is the second stage; the second stage is the third stage."

"In the quiescent True Suchness (tathatā), what sequence could there be? Furthermore, another master stated: "In the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), sudden awakening means that reaching the tenth stage of abiding (shizhu) is identical to the tenth ground (shidi);

as for the mention of ten practices (shixing), ten transferences (shihuixiang), and ten grounds, these are merely redundant explanations. The intention behind these various interpretations is that they all represent partial or biased understandings.
In the merely equal Dharma-realm, there is as yet no discussion of awakening or non-awakening; how, then, could one discuss shallowness or depth?
To speak of awakening where there is no awakening is to speak of shallowness and depth where there is neither shallowness nor depth.

Upon examining the various Mahāyāna sūtras for their ultimate clarification of principle, none surpasses the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* in elucidating the equality of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Although there is neither speech nor demonstration therein, the stages and practices of the bodhisattvas ultimately shine forth with brilliant clarity.
Therefore, we shall now revert to a concise enumeration of seven stages to clarify the positions of the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

First, regarding the Ten Faiths (*shixin*): if those of sharp faculties attain sudden enlightenment through profound and wondrous roots of goodness, and upon hearing it taught that "all sentient beings are themselves Great Nirvāṇa and cannot be extinguished further;

all sentient beings possess the marks of Bodhi," they immediately give rise to great kindness and great compassion. Taking the four unconditioned (*wu zuo*) Real Truths as their object, they initiate the Four Great Vows. This is called the arousal of the Bodhicitta according to the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding "faith": it is to believe that all sentient beings are themselves true nature and liberation, fully possessing the Three Jewels in one essence and the threefold contemplation in one mind;
to contemplate the principles of the two truths and the three truths, attaining unimpeded penetration and achieving a mind of sympathetic joy—this is the cause for the five grades of disciples.
If one further attains samādhi and dhāraṇī, and the six sense organs become pure, this constitutes entry into the stage of the ten faiths.

If one achieves the Ten Faiths, one is then able to perceive the principle of the True Truth (paramārtha-satya) and sever the views and afflictions within the realm of desire; furthermore, one can perceive the principle of the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya), discerning the phenomena of the ten dharma-realms with a mind free from error or confusion, giving rise to an understanding of the "concordant Middle Way" and subduing the ignorance beyond the realms.
Therefore, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattvas of the ten wholesome paths, having resolved upon the Great Mind, forever depart from the ocean of the wheel of suffering in the three realms.
The *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies the purity of the mental faculty, stating:
"Although he has not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna), his faculty of mind (manas-indriya) is already purified to such an extent.
Second, the clarification of the stages of the ten abidings (daśa-vihāra) consists of two parts:
first, a brief explanation of the stage of the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment (prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra).
Second, the categories apply to all nine abodes.
First, regarding the formal explanation of the stage of the Initial Resolve Abode (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*): it is called the "Resolve Abode" because three kinds of resolve are generated;
the Nirvāṇa of the Three Virtues (*triguṇanirvāṇa*) is termed the "abode."
What are called the three kinds of mental arousal?
First, the arousal of a wholesome mind through the condition of the object;
second, the arousal of a mind of wisdom through the condition of realization.
Third, the mind is aroused through the principle of the direct cause (*hetu*).

First, regarding the arousal of the mind through the good causes of conditions (*pratyaya*): all the roots of goodness that sentient beings have cultivated throughout immeasurable kalpas—such as bowing the head, joining the palms, snapping the fingers, scattering flowers, arousing the bodhicitta, practicing compassion and making vows, and engaging in giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration—all these are simultaneously brought forth, such that the mind fully possesses the myriad practices and all the *pāramitās*.

Second, regarding the awakening of the wisdom-mind as the cause of realization: throughout immeasurable kalpas, sentient beings have heard even a single verse of the Mahāyāna; by upholding, reciting, explaining, transcribing, and practicing it through contemplative cultivation, all their accumulated wisdom is suddenly and simultaneously developed, becoming the true, untainted state.

Third, regarding the mind that arises through the principle of the direct cause: since beginningless time, the Buddha-nature and true mind of sentient beings have been constantly obscured and covered by ignorance; when the powers of the two causes—the conditional and the penetrating—shatter the darkness of ignorance, it is suddenly and perfectly revealed.
The development of these three kinds of mind is therefore called "arousing the mind" (bodhicitta).
As for "abiding," it refers to abiding in the nirvāṇa of the three virtues:
first, the Dharma-body; second, prajñā; and third, liberation.
These three are neither vertical nor horizontal, like the worldly letter "I" (ī), and are thus called the Secret Treasury.
When the true mind arises, it is the Dharmakāya;
when the discerning cause-mind arises, it is Prajñā.
When the causal mind arises, it is itself liberation.

If these three minds arise, they are like the worldly letter "I" (ī). One who is provisionally called a practitioner abides in these three minds by means of the dharma of non-abiding; this is precisely to abide in the secret treasury of the three virtues of nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is called the "Abiding in the Initial Arising of the Mind."

If one abides in the three virtues, this is to abide in inconceivable liberation; it is to abide in the Mahāyāna; it is to abide in the Prajñāpāramitā by means of the dharma of non-abiding; it is to abide in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

To cultivate and maintain this within the mind, like empty space, is to abide in the dharma-nature (dharmatā), to abide in the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), to abide in suchness (tathatā), to abide in the Tathāgatagarbha, to abide in the Middle Way and the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), to abide in the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and to abide in ultimate emptiness (atyantaśūnyatā). It is to abide in great loving-kindness and great compassion, the ten powers (daśabala), the four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), and the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇikadharma); it is to abide in the four unhindered knowledges (pratisaṃvid), the supernormal powers (abhijñā), the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), all the pāramitās, and all the gates of samādhis and dhāraṇīs.
To state the essentials: this refers to abiding in the two bodies—the True Body (dharmakāya) and the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya)—which comprise all Buddha-dharmas.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one immediately attains perfect awakening."
Having thoroughly realized the true nature of all phenomena, they understand the Dharma they hear through their own awakening rather than by depending on others.
These Bodhisattvas have accomplished ten kinds of power of wisdom; they are ultimately free from delusion and untainted like space;
their pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serene and responds to all things.

You should know that this is precisely the arousal of true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), which severs the first grade of ignorance (*avidyā*). It is what this sutra clarifies as "knowing all dharmas in a single thought-moment," and it is "the attainment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Furthermore, it is what this sutra clarifies as "entering the gate of non-dual dharmas (*advayadharmamukha*) and attaining the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*)."

Second, regarding the analogical explanation of the nine abodes: as in this first abode, the three contemplations manifest before one; with effortless application of mind, one severs, moment by moment, the immeasurable categories of ignorance within the dharma-realm in numbers beyond calculation.

Broadly speaking, this is summarized as ten grades of wisdom and abandonment, which correspond to the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*). Thus, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "Entering into the prajñā of principle is called an abode. This refers to ten successive advancements of untainted, true illumination, whereby one enters together with the principle of the Middle Way, the Buddha-nature, and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). By means of the dharma of non-abiding, one proceeds from the shallow to the deep, abiding in the principle of the Buddha’s threefold virtue and nirvana;
these are the ten grades of wisdom that abide in all Buddha-dharmas, and are therefore called the Ten Abodes.

Third, the clarification of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*): this very true mind of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) possesses all practices within a single mind. From moment to moment, it spontaneously advances and flows into the ocean of the equal Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It shatters the ten grades of ignorance (*avidyā*), realizes the ten grades of wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), and all practices and *pāramitās* naturally increase. It gives rise to the merit of self-cultivation and transforming others that is equal to empty space and the Dharma-realm; therefore, they are called the Ten Practices.

Fourth, regarding the clarification of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*): with the true illumination of the single mind, understanding and practice unfold in every thought-moment, and each mind is quiescent and extinguished. Thus, one naturally turns back and enters the equal Dharma-realm and the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Furthermore, by further advancing to shatter the ten grades of ignorance and realize the ten grades of wisdom and abandonment, they are called the "ten dedications."

Fifth, the clarification of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*): When the untainted true illumination enters the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*), it is like the great earth, capable of producing all Buddha-dharmas, bearing the burden of sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*, and universally entering the ground of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. It is as vast as the *dharmadhātu* and ultimate as empty space;
furthermore, by advancing to break through the ten grades of ignorance and advancing to realize the ten grades of wisdom and abandonment, one is thereby said to have clarified the "Ten Grounds."

Sixth, regarding the clarification of the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*): having exhausted the source of ignorance (*avidyā*) and entered the gate of profound mystery, the wisdom of the ultimate limit is fulfilled and becomes ultimately pure. Having ascended to the summit of the mountain of the Middle Way, one parts from the parents of ignorance; this is still the "diamond-like unobstructed [wisdom] of the final mind" (*paścima-citta-vajra-anāvaraṇa*), which is termed "that which has something to be severed" and is called the "Superior Being" (*uttama-puruṣa*).
Seventh, regarding the elucidation of the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue-di*): because it is ultimate liberation and the unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom, it is said:
"That which has nothing further to be severed is called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*)."
"This is precisely the ultimate final mind, wherein the three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal; it is Great Nirvana.
'Great Nirvana' is named the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas—vertically deep and horizontally vast—and is able to universally transform sentient beings through twenty-five samādhis;
its ten successive manifestations of benefitting beings are ultimately universal and pervasive."
For example, if the roots of a great tree are extremely deep, its branches and twigs will also be large.

If the wisdom of the true mark (dharmatā) exhausts the source and reaches the very nature of things, then the merit of its transformative function will fill the entire dharma-realm; its boundlessly great utility is ultimately perfect and complete.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha has come from the Great Path of Prajñā-pāramitā; the Buddha has reached the bottom of the deep ocean of Prajñā-pāramitā. The *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Beyond 'Ta,' there are no words that can be spoken. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Non-arising and non-arising cannot be described."

If one were to distinguish the stages based on this, then the thirty moments of mind prior to [the first bhūmi] are all the stage of the inconceivable, without sequential order, which is quiescent true suchness and the equal dharma-realm.
Question:
From which sutras or treatises does such a stage of perfection originate? Answer:
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies that "the Moon-Love Samādhi (*candrakānta-samādhi*) gradually increases its radiance from the first day to the fifteenth day;
furthermore, from the sixteenth day to the thirtieth day, its radiance gradually diminishes until it is exhausted."
